topic: Getting more Google enquiries without ads
title: How can a tradesman get more enquiries from Google without paying for ads?
description: A practical guide for tradespeople on getting found on Google and turning searches into calls and enquiries, without paying for ads.
card: The free, practical steps that get a trades firm found on Google and turning searches into calls, in the order worth doing them.
summary: You get more enquiries from Google without ads by being easy for Google to understand and easy for a customer to trust. Fill in your Google Business Profile properly, give each main service and town its own clear page on your website, show real jobs with real photos, collect reviews steadily, keep the site fast on a phone, and reply to enquiries quickly. None of it costs ad money, but it does take some weeks to show.

sections.heading: How Google decides who to show for a trade search
paragraphs: When someone types something like "roofer near me" or "driveway installer in Maidstone", Google usually shows two things: a map with a short list of local firms, and the normal website results underneath. Each is judged a bit differently, and you want to appear in both.

For the map, Google looks at how well your profile matches the search, how close you are to the customer, and how well known and trusted you seem. For the normal results, it looks at whether a page on your site clearly answers what the person asked. So your job is simple to state: make it obvious what you do, where you do it, and that real customers rate you.

sections.heading: Start with your Google Business Profile
paragraphs: For most local trades, the free Google Business Profile does more work than anything else you can set up. It is what appears on the map, and it is often where the customer taps the call button without ever opening your website.

Get the basics exactly right: your business name as it is used day to day, the correct service area, your main category plus any others that genuinely apply, opening hours, and a phone number you answer. Then add photos of finished jobs, not stock images. We go through this step by step in [Google Business Profile for tradesmen](/guides/google-business-profile-for-tradesmen).

Keep your name, phone number and website address the same everywhere they appear, including Facebook, directories and your van. Mismatches make it harder for Google to be confident it is one real business.

sections.heading: Make your website say what you do and where
paragraphs: The most common reason a trades website does not show up is that it says very little. A homepage reading "quality workmanship, competitive prices" gives Google nothing to match against a search like "loft conversion Guildford".

Be specific, in plain words a customer would use. If you do resin driveways, say resin driveways. If you cover three towns and the villages around them, name them. A page per main service, and a clear page listing the areas you cover, gives Google something definite to show.

bullets.text: Do not squash roofing, guttering, fascias and flat roofs into one paragraph. Each deserves its own page with what is involved, the kind of job you do and how a customer gets a quote.
Mention where you work in headings and sentences, as in "Block paving driveways in Tunbridge Wells". Do not paste a list of fifty places at the bottom of every page; it reads badly and does not help.

bullets.lead: Put the title and heading to work.
bullets.text: The page title and main heading should include the service and the area, written as a person would say it.

bullets.lead: Put your phone number and a quote button at the top.
bullets.text: Someone who has found you should not have to hunt for how to get in touch.

sections.heading: Show real jobs, not just claims
paragraphs: Finished work is the best content a trades site can have. Customers trust a before-and-after more than any slogan, and a write-up of a real job naturally contains the words people search: the type of work, the town, the materials, the problem you solved.

After each decent job, take a few photos, then write a short account: where it was, what the customer wanted, what you did and anything tricky you dealt with. A few honest paragraphs is plenty. Ask the customer if you can use the photos, and avoid showing house numbers or anything that identifies them without permission.

Over time this builds up a body of pages that each match a different search, and it makes your site look like a busy, active firm. It is also what stops you looking like everyone else in the next town.

sections.heading: Collect reviews steadily
paragraphs: Reviews affect both whether you appear and whether the customer picks you once you do. Steady and recent beats a burst once a year. The easiest habit is to ask at the end of every job, while the customer is happy, and send them a direct link so it takes seconds.

When a review arrives, reply politely, good or bad. A calm reply to a poor review often says more about you than the review itself. Our guide on [how to get more Google reviews](/guides/how-to-get-more-google-reviews) covers the wording to use and how to make asking feel natural.

sections.heading: Keep the site fast and usable on a phone
paragraphs: Most people searching for a tradesperson are on a phone, often in a hurry and sometimes with poor signal. If your site takes ages to load, or the buttons are tiny, they go back to the results and try the next firm.

Large uncompressed photos are the usual culprit, followed by heavy page-builder code and too many add-ons. Resize photos before uploading, keep pages simple, and check how it looks and behaves on your own phone, not just a computer. You can run your site through our [free website speed test](/speed-test), which uses Google's own testing tool and stores nothing.

If the site is slow because of how it was built, no amount of tweaking will fully fix it. That is one of the differences covered in [Wix or a hand-coded website](/guides/wix-or-hand-coded-website-for-tradesmen).

sections.heading: Reply quickly and make enquiring easy
paragraphs: Getting found is only half of it. If the enquiry form is long, or the reply takes days, you lose the job to whoever answered first. Keep the form short: name, phone number, what they want done and where. Add a tap-to-call number and a WhatsApp link if you use it for work.

Make sure enquiries reach your phone straight away rather than sitting in an inbox you check once a week. A fast, friendly first reply, even just to say you have seen it and when you will call, puts you ahead of many firms.

sections.heading: What to expect, and what to check
paragraphs: None of this works overnight. After you change your profile, add pages or collect reviews, give it several weeks before judging. Google needs time to find and trust the changes, and local rankings move slowly.

Keep a simple record: how many calls and enquiries you get each month, and ask every new customer how they found you. That tells you more than any report. If enquiries stay low after a few months of steady effort, work through [why your website is not getting enquiries](/guides/website-not-getting-enquiries) to find where the problem is.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get enquiries from Google without ads?
faqs.a: Expect weeks rather than days, and often a few months for pages and reviews to build up. A well-filled Google Business Profile can start to help sooner than website changes.

faqs.q: Do I need a website if I have a Google Business Profile?
faqs.a: A profile can bring calls on its own, but a website gives you somewhere to show your work, list your services and areas, and rank for more searches. The two work best together.

faqs.q: Is it worth paying for Google Ads as well?
faqs.a: Ads can bring work quickly, but they stop the moment you stop paying. Getting your profile, site and reviews right first means any ad money you do spend lands on something that converts.

faqs.q: How many towns should I mention on my website?
faqs.a: Name the places you genuinely want and are able to work in, ideally with real jobs to show for them. A long list of towns pasted in does not help and can look careless.

faqs.q: Can I do this myself without any technical skill?
faqs.a: Yes. Filling in your Business Profile, taking good job photos, asking for reviews and replying fast need no technical knowledge. The website side is easier if the site lets you add or change pages simply.
